passages.original: iturus autem quam rediturus dixissem securius propter eos, qui putant animos humanos pro meritis peccatorum suorum de caelo . lapsos seu deiectos in corpora ista detrudi. sed ego propterea non dubitaui dicere, quia ita dixi in caelum, tamquam dicerem ad deum, qui eius est auctor et conditor, sicut beatus Cyprianus non cunctatus est dicere: nam cum corpus e terra, spiritum possideamus e caelo, ipsi terra et caelum sumus. et in libro Ecclesiastae scriptum. est:_ spiritus reuertatur ad deum, qui dedit illum quod utique sic ,.. intellegendum est, ut non resistatur apostolo dicenti nondum natos nihil egisse boni aut mali.
passages.english: But I would have said "about to go" rather than "about to return" more safely, because of those who think that human souls, having fallen or been cast down from heaven on account of the deserts of their sins, are thrust down into these bodies. But I did not hesitate to say it for this reason: that I said "into heaven" as though I were saying "to God," who is its author and founder, just as the blessed Cyprian did not hesitate to say: "For since we possess the body from earth and the spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven." And in the book of Ecclesiastes it is written: "Let the spirit return to God, who gave it." This must certainly be understood in such a way that there is no contradiction of the apostle, who says that those not yet born had done nothing good or evil.
passages.notes: Stray punctuation in the edition ("caelo .", "scriptum. est:_", ",..") is treated as scanning noise.

passages.original: quod dixi: dei bonitas omnia deficientia sic ordinat, ut ibi sint, ubi congruentissime possint esse, donec ordinatis motibus ad id recurrant, unde defecerunt, non sic accipiendum est, tamquam omnia recurrant ad id, unde defecerunt, sicut Origeni uisum est, sed ea omnia, quae recurrunt. non enim recurrent ad deum, a quo defecerunt, qui sempiterno igne punientur, quamuis omnia deficientia sic ordinentur, ut ibi sint, ubi congruentissime possint esse, quia et illi, qui non recurrunt, congruentissime in poena sunt.
passages.english: What I said, "The goodness of God so orders all things that fall away that they are where they can most fittingly be, until by ordered movements they return to that from which they fell away," is not to be taken as though all things return to that from which they fell away, as Origen held, but [as meaning] all those things that do return. For those who will be punished with everlasting fire will not return to God, from whom they fell away, although all things that fall away are so ordered that they are where they can most fittingly be, since those too who do not return are most fittingly in punishment.

passages.original: si autem ipsa pulchritudo in omnibus corporibus intellegatur, cogit ista sententia etiam ipsum mundum animal credere, ut etiam in ipsum, quod in illo imitatur constantiam, a summo deo per animam traiciatur. sed animal esse istum mundum, sicut Plato sensit aliique philosophi plurimi, nec ratione certa indagare potui nec diuinarum scripturarum auctoritate persuaderi posse cognoui. unde, tale aliquid a me dictum quod accipi possit etiam in libro de inmortalitate animae, temere dictum notaui, non quia hoc falsum esse confirmo, sed quia nec uerum esse conprehendo, quod sit animal mundus.
passages.english: But if beauty itself is understood [to be] in all bodies, this statement forces [one] to believe that even the world itself is a living being, so that into it too, that in it which imitates constancy is conveyed from the supreme God through a soul. But that this world is a living being, as Plato and very many other philosophers held, I have neither been able to establish by certain reasoning nor found that it can be proved by the authority of the divine scriptures. Hence, where something of the kind was said by me that could be so taken, also in the book On the Immortality of the Soul, I have marked it as rashly said, not because I affirm this to be false, but because I do not grasp it to be true, that the world is a living being.

passages.original: In quo dixi quodam loco de apostolo Petro, quod in illo tam-quam in petra fundata sit ecclesia. qui sensus etiam cantatur ore multorum in uersibus beatissimi Ambrosi, ubi de gallo gallinacio ait: hoc ipse, petra ecclesiae,canente culpam diluit. sed scio me postea saepissime sic exposuisse, quod a domino dictum est: tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam, ut super hunc intellegeretur, quem confessus est Petrus dicens: tu es Christus, filius dei uiui, ac sic Petrus ab hac petra appellatus personam ecclesiae figuraret, quae super hanc petram aedificatur et accepit claues regni caelorum.
passages.english: In it I said in a certain place about the apostle Peter that the church was founded on him as on a rock. This sense is also sung by the mouths of many in the verses of the most blessed Ambrose, where he says of the cock: "At its crowing, he himself, the rock of the church, washed away his guilt." But I know that afterwards I very often explained what was said by the Lord, "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church," in such a way that "on this" should be understood as him whom Peter confessed, saying, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," and that thus Peter, named from this rock, represented the person of the church, which is built upon this rock and has received the keys of the kingdom of heaven.
passages.notes: "In quo" refers to a work named in the preceding (missing) heading; in the Retractationes this is the work against the letter of the Donatist (Contra epistulam Donati).

passages.original: in quo uerba quaedam, quae uelut Xysti Romani episcopi et martyris Pelagius posuit, ita defendi, tamquam re uera eiusdem Xysti essent; id enim putaueram. sed postea legi Sexti philosophi esse, non Xysti Christiani.
passages.english: In this [work] I defended certain words which Pelagius had set down as being those of Xystus, bishop of Rome and martyr, as though they really were the words of that same Xystus; for that is what I had thought. But afterwards I read that they are by Sextus the philosopher, not by Xystus the Christian.
passages.notes: The work referred to is not named in the passage; in the Retractations this remark concerns Augustine's De natura et gratia. 'Xystus' is Pope Sixtus II, the martyr. 'Sextus the philosopher' is the author of the Sentences of Sextus, a collection of maxims.
